extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners (attorneys/agents) preparing or prosecuting AI-related patent applications
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative standards for drafting, prosecuting, and assessing patent claims and specifications directed to AI- and computer-implemented inventions, with attention to Section 101/112 issues, detectability, and ethical considerations. Focuses on what to claim and how to describe technical improvements, implementation details, and non-legal risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice / two-part eligibility (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that are merely abstract ideas (e.g., mathematical concepts and certain methods of organizing human activity) are patent-ineligible unless they include 'significantly more.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the two-part Alice test: (1) determine whether the claim is directed to an abstract idea (mathematical concept, mental process, or method of organizing human activity); (2) if so, determine whether additional elements transform the claim into a patent-eligible application (i.e., provide an 'inventive concept' or 'significantly more'). The specification should describe how the claimed invention provides an improvement to the technical field to support eligibility (e.g., the Specification describes that using DeepSpeech learning ... achieves higher performance than traditional methods).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must recite technical implementation (not just formulas)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical formulas in the specification are not sufficient if the mathematical formulas are 'not recited in the claims.' Claims should be directed to a specific implementation comprising technical elements (e.g., AI and computer speech recognition) rather than abstract formulas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claims merely recite computations or formulas without tying them to a particular technical implementation, the Examiner/PTAB may find them to be abstract. Draft claims to include technical elements or steps that show how the computation is performed in a concrete system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid language that makes claims 'methods of organizing human activity'
rubrics_metrics.description: Terminology such as 'contract document' or other labels tied to legal/administrative interactions can make claims vulnerable to subject-matter-ineligibility as 'methods of organizing human activity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious when claiming operations framed as legal or business interactions; consider recasting claims to emphasize technical mechanisms or improvements rather than the human/social/legal activity itself (Ex parte Coquard).

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvements in computing must be to the computers/technology, not just to tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments that a claim 'improves computing' are unpersuasive if the specification describes only using generic computing devices to perform the task; the claim must represent an improvement in the computers themselves or computer functionality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show that claimed features change how the computer operates (unconventional architecture, specialized hardware, concrete routines) rather than merely using a generic computer as a tool to perform a mental or organizational task (PTAB reasoning in Coquard and related cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental processes judicial exception (claims performable by human mind)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim steps that can be performed in the human mind are a judicial exception (mental processes) and can render claims ineligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If claim elements can be performed mentally (even if also recited as performed electronically), the claim may be directed to a mental process. Showing a concrete computer-rooted implementation and explaining why performance cannot practically be done in the mind helps. Merely reciting storage or a processor is insufficient to overcome this if other claim elements can be done mentally (Ex parte Vasey, Kerr).

rubrics_metrics.name: Broad claim scope that covers mental performance remains ineligible unless impractical to perform mentally
rubrics_metrics.description: If, under its broadest reasonable interpretation, a claim covers performance in the mind except for generic computer recitations, it remains in the mental processes category unless the claim cannot practically be performed in the mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid claim language that, when broadly read, permits purely mental performance; instead, narrow or add concrete, computer-specific limitations showing practical impossibility of mental performance (Ex parte Kerr).

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide detailed implementation of computer/ML elements (enablement and eligibility support)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent specification should provide sufficient detail of how computer/ML elements are implemented (hardware, functional requirements, flowcharts, unconventional routines) to avoid being characterized as 'well-understood, routine, and conventional.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include detailed disclosures (e.g., flow charts, specific hardware or software architecture, concrete routines) that explain how each claimed element operates; lack of such detail supports a finding that additional elements are conventional and do not supply 'significantly more.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reciting mere calculations without describing supporting circuitry
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that 'merely recite performing certain calculations without detailing any particular hardware circuitry' can be viewed as mathematical steps performable with pen and paper and therefore as abstract ideas or mental processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tie computational steps to specific hardware or constrained computing contexts that transform the mathematical operation into a practical application (Ex parte Rupp).

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic 'device' recitations without detail are conventional
rubrics_metrics.description: If the specification illustrates a device only as a generic box and does not describe details, a claimed device (e.g., 'chromatography analysis device') may be considered well-understood, routine, or conventional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe the device components, their interconnection, and how they operate in detail to show the device is not merely a generic conventional element (Ex parte Harada).

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement: specification must enable the full scope claimed (Amgen principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a patent claims an entire class of processes, machines, or structures, the specification must enable a person skilled in the art to make and use the entire class; 'the more one claims, the more one must enable.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide disclosure sufficient to avoid undue experimentation across the full scope of the claims. Broad 'genus' claims require commensurately broad enabling disclosure; conclusory assertions of enablement are insufficient (In re Starrett, Amgen citation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe 'how' claimed functional results are achieved (claims must identify how)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims cannot simply state a functional result; they should identify 'how' the functional result is achieved by limiting claim scope to concrete structures or concrete actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit claims to particular techniques, rules, structures, or concrete actions and include supporting description in the specification explaining the mechanisms by which the results are obtained (Realtime Data v. Array Networks; Am. Axle & Mfg. citation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid result-oriented claim drafting lacking inner functionality
rubrics_metrics.description: Result-oriented claims that could be performed with pen and paper and fail to recite inner functionality are likely directed to abstract ideas and vulnerable under Section 101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft claims that recite internal steps, data structures, or mechanisms rather than high-level results; include specificity in claim and specification about how mapping/annotation/ordering functions are implemented (IBM v. Zillow).

rubrics_metrics.name: Detectability as a value/claim-drafting consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent is more valuable if infringement is easily detectable. Detectable features are observable from the use, appearance, or construction of a product or process embodying an AI invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and claim features observable at inference (during operation), publicly disclosed materials (papers, specs, advertising), or aspects amenable to reverse-engineering. Consider claiming inputs/outputs, prompting behavior, or observable interactions that reveal the presence of the claimed AI feature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim and document features exposed at different lifecycle stages (dataflow/edge vs cloud)
rubrics_metrics.description: AI features can be detected at several stages including data collection, training, testing, and operation; features may be exposed differently when workload is split between edge devices and centralized compute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When claiming ML inventions, pay particular attention to the dataflow between centralized compute resources and edge devices; claim observable communication, interfaces, or distributed processing aspects that aid detectability and enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of public disclosures and reverse-engineering for detectability
rubrics_metrics.description: AI features may be detectable via public documents (academic publications, user guides, advertising) or reverse-engineering; SaaS products complicate reverse-engineering but publicly available data or structures may expose inputs/outputs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft specification/claims to tie inventive aspects to publicly observable behaviors or published details where possible, and consider strategies to preserve evidence of use for enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards-body considerations and FRAND/royalty constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard bodies (ANSI, IEEE, 3GPP, etc.) have patent policies that may require disclosure of relevant patents and may impose FRAND or royalty-free commitments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider contributing patented technologies to standards with awareness of disclosure and licensing obligations; evaluate strategic implications of standardization on licensing and enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid definitive safety/effectiveness claims in patent applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not make definitive statements that the underlying invention 'is safe', 'error free', or similarly absolute claims, as these can create product liability exposure or public scrutiny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use cautious factual language about datasets, testing, and performance. Use terms like 'inhibits safety issues' or 'enhances the likelihood of an accurate prediction' and avoid categorical guarantees (Practice Tip under Safe and Effective).

rubrics_metrics.name: Algorithmic discrimination protections and disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Systems should be designed to include 'proactive equity assessments' and 'use of representative data' to protect against bias; patent practitioners should counsel inventors on measures to avoid discriminatory algorithms and disclose such measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask inventors whether the system assesses people and how it addresses bias; disclose proactive measures and datasets used to train models in the specification to both reduce third-party discrimination claims and provide potential claimable elements (Practice Tip under Algorithmic Discrimination Protections).

rubrics_metrics.name: Data privacy cautiousness in drafting
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure data collection conforms to reasonable expectations; avoid broadening claims to encompass sensitive personal data and be cautious when describing types of data used in AI applications (HIPAA and other restrictions may apply).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit and define data-related claim language for sensitive domains, describe consent/usage boundaries where relevant, and avoid wording that implies abusive data practices. Consider legal/regulatory constraints and the Blueprint's guidance when drafting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice and explanation — disclose user notification and explanations where relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: Users should know why and how an AI system made its determination; providing plain-language explanations and notice of automated decision-making can be important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where an AI makes determinations that impact people, consider including disclosure that the user is notified, that automation is used, and mechanisms (plain-language explanations, who is responsible) to support later compliance and public trust (Practice Tip under Notice and Explanation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Human alternatives, consideration, and fallback mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Automated systems should provide people a choice to opt out of AI decision-making and have fallback access to a human for review or appeal, especially in sensitive domains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For inventions likely to be used in sensitive domains, describe human-in-the-loop options, override mechanisms, appeal pathways, or other fallback procedures in the specification to show consideration of human alternatives and mitigate risk (Practice Tip under Human Alternatives, Consideration, and Fallback).
